student_thinking: Identify the placebo problem: only the medication group has expectations of improvement
Identify the rater problem: clinicians know the groups and may rate with bias
Choose the double-blind placebo design and reject changes that leave either problem

key_conditions.condition: the stem supplies every fact needed and exactly one option follows from all of the steps

No pill leaves patient expectations uncontrolled, and clinicians who know the groups can still bias ratings.

steps: Identify the placebo problem: only the medication group has expectations of improvement

payload.explanation_en:
The correct answer is Give comparison patients an identical inert pill, and keep patients and the clinicians who rate anxiety unaware of who gets which.. A placebo control equates expectations in both groups, and keeping patients and raters unaware prevents expectations from affecting reports and ratings.
Compare the medication group with a group of people who have no anxiety to see whether the two groups' ratings become similar. is incorrect: A group without anxiety is not a comparison for treatment effects and does not control for expectations.
Have the patients taking the medication rate their own improvement more often so that the clinicians' expectations matter less to the results. is incorrect: More frequent self-reports leave expectations about the medication, and the lack of a placebo comparison, unaddressed.
Give comparison patients no pill but let the clinicians know the groups, so that clinicians can monitor side effects more closely. is incorrect: No pill leaves patient expectations uncontrolled, and clinicians who know the groups can still bias ratings.

payload.stem: A researcher compares problem-solving test scores of 25-year-olds, 45-year-olds, and 65-year-olds tested in the same month. The 65-year-olds score lowest. Which is the most important limitation on concluding that problem-solving declines as people age?

options.text: The same participants were tested at three ages, so practice with the test may have raised the scores of the older participants.
options.why: This describes a longitudinal design; the researcher tested different people at one time, not the same people repeatedly.

options.text: The study did not use random assignment to the age groups, so the researcher cannot compute a correlation between age and scores.
options.why: Age groups cannot be assigned and a correlation can still be computed; the limit is about cohort differences, not computation.

options.text: The age groups were born in different eras and may differ in education and experience, so cohort effects may explain the gaps.
options.why: A cross-sectional design compares different people at one time, so differences between age groups may reflect generation rather than aging itself.

options.text: The 65-year-olds took the test at the same time as the others, so time of testing was a confound that favored the younger groups.
options.why: Everyone was tested in the same month, so time of testing was constant and cannot explain the group differences.

payload.stem: A longitudinal study follows 200 adults from age 20 to age 60 to see how life satisfaction changes. By age 60, 80 participants have left the study, and most of them had reported low life satisfaction at earlier ages. What is the most likely effect of this attrition?

options.text: The remaining participants may overestimate satisfaction at 60, because people with lower satisfaction tended to leave.
options.why: When dropouts differ systematically from those who stay, the remaining sample no longer represents the original group and can bias the later results.

options.text: The results become more reliable, because the participants who remain form a more homogeneous group with similar life experiences.
options.why: A more homogeneous remaining group is a biased sample, not a more reliable one, because the dropouts are not random.

options.text: The study becomes a cross-sectional design, because fewer participants are measured at age 60 than were measured at age 20.
options.why: A design is longitudinal when the same people are followed over time; losing participants does not change the design.

options.text: The results are unaffected, because the dropouts' earlier scores are still included in the analysis of changes across the years.
options.why: Dropouts' earlier scores do not describe their later satisfaction, so conclusions about age 60 remain biased.

payload.stem: A researcher draws a random sample of 1,000 adults from a national list and asks how many hours each volunteers per month and how satisfied each is with life. People who volunteer more report higher satisfaction. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The relationship applies only to the 1,000 adults surveyed, because the researcher did not randomly assign participants to volunteer or not.
options.why: Random assignment is needed for cause; generalizing to the population depends on the random sample, which was used.

options.text: There is no relationship in the population, because a correlation from a survey of self-reported hours and satisfaction is always unreliable.
options.why: A survey correlation can be meaningful; the limits are about cause and self-report bias, not a proof of no relationship.

options.text: Volunteering causes higher life satisfaction in adults nationally, because the random sample makes it possible to conclude cause as well as generalize.
options.why: Random sampling supports generalization but not causation; the researcher did not manipulate volunteering.

options.text: The relationship probably holds for adults nationally, but the study cannot show that volunteering causes higher life satisfaction.
options.why: A random sample supports generalizing to the population, while the correlational design leaves cause and direction unsettled.

payload.stem: Researchers want to survey 15-year-olds about bullying at school and quote some responses in a published article. Which procedure best follows ethical guidelines?

options.text: Tell students only that the survey is about school life, and reveal the topic of bullying only in the published article afterward.
options.why: Hiding the main topic from participants prevents informed consent and is not justified for a low-risk survey.

options.text: Obtain parental permission and student assent, explain the right to stop at any time, and keep responses anonymous or confidential.

options.text: Ask students to sign their names to every survey so that responses can be checked, and tell them that they must finish the survey.
options.why: Signed surveys reduce confidentiality, and participants must be free to stop at any time.

options.text: Obtain only the principal's permission, because the survey takes place at school, and publish quotes with each student's first name.
options.why: A principal's approval does not replace parental permission and student assent, and names break confidentiality.

payload.stem: A researcher wants to study how people respond when an actor pretends to need help, without telling participants in advance that the emergency is staged. Which procedure would best make this use of deception ethically acceptable?

options.text: Use deception only with participants who have taken a research methods course, so that no consent form is needed for the session.
options.why: Prior knowledge of research methods does not remove the need for review, consent, and debriefing.

options.text: Pay participants a larger fee to compensate for the deception, which removes the need for institutional review of the procedure.
options.why: Payment does not replace ethical review or debriefing and cannot justify risky deception.

options.text: Let participants decide after the session whether their data may be used, without explaining that the emergency was staged.
options.why: Without a debriefing about the staging, participants remain deceived, whatever they decide about their data.

options.text: Obtain institutional review approval showing the deception is necessary and low in risk, and debrief participants afterward.
options.why: Deception can be acceptable when review finds it justified and low in risk and participants are fully debriefed afterward.

student_thinking: Compare spaced with massed study within each sleep condition
Compare 8 hours with under 6 hours within each study method
Choose the conclusion that holds in both comparisons and reject answers that rely on only the best or worst group

key_conditions.condition: spaced beats massed in both sleep conditions and full sleep beats short sleep in both study methods

misconceptions.description: Compares only the worst group; spaced study also gave a higher number passing within each sleep condition.
Compares only the best group; the full-sleep groups also passed more often than the short-sleep groups within each study method.
Spaced study also gave a higher number passing among the short-sleep students, so its benefit was not limited to full sleep.

verification.independent_path: every number and the key are computed by code from the data shown (statistics module) and recomputed with numpy; wrong options are the standard slips (mean for median, forgetting to sort, range for spread)

judgment_demand: apply the concept to the scenario

steps: Compare spaced with massed study within each sleep condition
Compare 8 hours with under 6 hours within each study method
Choose the conclusion that holds in both comparisons and reject answers that rely on only the best or worst group

payload.explanation_en:
The correct answer is More passed with spaced study in both sleep conditions (31 vs 22; 24 vs 17), and more passed after 8 hours of sleep in both study methods.. Compare the two study methods within each sleep column and the two sleep conditions within each study row; both factors show an advantage in both comparisons.
Only sleep mattered among these students, because the lowest number who passed was in a group that slept under 6 hours before the quiz. is incorrect: Compares only the worst group; spaced study also gave a higher number passing within each sleep condition.
Only the study method mattered among these students, because the highest number who passed was in a group that used spaced study. is incorrect: Compares only the best group; the full-sleep groups also passed more often than the short-sleep groups within each study method.
Spaced study helped only the students who slept 8 hours, because the short-sleep students passed less often than the full-sleep students did. is incorrect: Spaced study also gave a higher number passing among the short-sleep students, so its benefit was not limited to full sleep.

scope_skill.notes: Table reading on sleep and study effects; fits 3.C reasonably and 1.5 acceptably. Counts are descriptive, but random assignment supports the causal wording.

key_scoring.notes: A is uniquely correct: 31>22, 24>17 and 31>24, 22>17. B, C and D are each contradicted by the table.

stimulus_expression.notes: Table is complete, group size is stated, and the wording is clear.

distractor_explanation.notes: Distractors encode distinct slips (worst group only, best group only, false interaction) and each is explained. A is somewhat longer than the others, a minor cue.

exam_suitability.notes: About 100 s, light arithmetic, no calculator, four options.

review.summary: Sound two-way table-reading item with a unique correct answer, plausible distractors, and appropriate load. Passes.

difficulty.label: exam_prep
difficulty.rationale: Student must (1) compare spaced vs massed within each sleep condition, (2) compare 8 hr vs under 6 hr within each study method, and (3) judge which option's claim holds across both factors, rejecting single-factor and interaction claims. This combines reading a 2x2 table with reasoning about two independent variables in a randomly assigned experiment. Option 4 survives the first comparison but fails when the short-sleep spaced vs massed counts are checked (24 vs 17). Arithmetic is light, reading is short, and no out-of-scope content is needed.

difficultyRationale: The student must read a 2x2 table and compare study methods within each sleep condition. They must then compare sleep conditions within each study method, and combine both comparisons to reject the near-miss options. The options that claim only one variable mattered or that spaced study helped only with full sleep fail on later checks. This meets the 3-step, 2-concept/source threshold for exam_prep. The scope is in range (sleep, data interpretation), the wording is clear, and the arithmetic is light.

payload.stem: Researchers randomly assigned 160 students to study by a spaced or a massed method and to sleep either 8 hours or under 6 hours before a quiz, with 40 students in each of the four groups. The table shows how many in each group passed. Which conclusion is best supported?

stimulus.description: Students who passed a quiz (out of 40 in each group)

options.text: Spaced study helped only the students who slept 8 hours, because the short-sleep students passed less often than the full-sleep students did.
options.why: Spaced study also gave a higher number passing among the short-sleep students, so its benefit was not limited to full sleep.

options.text: Only sleep mattered among these students, because the lowest number who passed was in a group that slept under 6 hours before the quiz.
options.why: Compares only the worst group; spaced study also gave a higher number passing within each sleep condition.

options.text: More passed with spaced study in both sleep conditions (36 vs 27; 28 vs 18), and more passed after 8 hours of sleep in both study methods.
options.why: Compare the two study methods within each sleep column and the two sleep conditions within each study row; both factors show an advantage in both comparisons.

options.text: Only the study method mattered among these students, because the highest number who passed was in a group that used spaced study.
options.why: Compares only the best group; the full-sleep groups also passed more often than the short-sleep groups within each study method.
